title: Beas & Loom
sub: A concept brand for the Kullu shawl: how to make a real craft’s value visible when the copies look the same.
description: Beas & Loom: a concept brand rebuild for the Kullu shawl, from research and positioning to identity and a live launch page. A Lab project by Riya Dutta.
facts: Concept brand. Beas & Loom is not a real company; the craft and the facts are.
The Kullu shawl, Himachal Pradesh (GI No. 19)
Research brief, positioning, identity and a launch page
Everything: research, strategy, identity, design and build

sections.title: Make real visible.
sections.lead: A buyer can’t tell a ₹300 power-loom shawl from a handwoven Kullu shawl at a glance, and the GI tag doesn’t help them.
paras: I set myself one brief: rebuild a heritage craft from home as a modern brand, without inventing anything. The craft, the problem and every fact are real; only the label is made up.

sections.title: What the copies are up against.

items.l: OF SHAWLS SOLD AS KULLU AND KINNAURI REPORTED TO BE MADE IN LUDHIANA FACTORIES
THE KULLU SHAWL’S GEOGRAPHICAL INDICATION, SINCE 2004

sections.note: Weavers say the GI tag hasn’t stopped the copies. The trusted name, the Bhuttico weavers’ cooperative (1944), sells handwoven shawls at about ₹2,700–3,200, with a cooperative, souvenir feel. Nobody sells the Kullu shawl as a modern heirloom. Sources: The Tribune (an older report), The Tribune, 2009, IP India, Bhuttico.

sections.title: How do you make real visible?

items.t: Every shawl carries a record: weaver, village, fibre. The brand sells certainty.
Kullu borders are woven freehand, never traced, so each one is a one-off. The brand sells rarity.
Freehand is the story; the record is the proof. One gives the feeling of luxury, the other earns the trust.

sections.title: Freehand is the story. The record is the proof.
sections.lead: For people who buy fewer, better things and want to know where they come from: the Kullu shawl made as a modern heirloom, woven by a named weaver and recorded so it can be trusted.

tiles.d: Handwoven on a pit or frame loom in the Kullu valley.
Every shawl carries its weaver’s name and village.
The border is woven freehand, and never repeated on purpose.

sections.close: The proof is physical and simple: a woven mark with the piece number in the selvedge, and a record card that travels with the shawl.

sections.title: Colour only at the border.
sections.note: The palette works the way the shawl does: a quiet ground, with all the colour at the edges. Cormorant Garamond for the name, a plain sans for the record, and a woven border band as the one recurring device.

sections.title: What I wouldn’t make up.
sections.intro: A brand about proving things are real can’t fake its own details.

items.d: The example record card leaves the weaver and village blank, and says why.
Pricing should start from a fair weaver wage, which needs real data first.
I couldn’t find a reliable source for how long one shawl takes, so the page doesn’t claim one.
No photos of real artisans without permission; illustration until there are my own.
Every page says Beas & Loom is not a real company.

sections.title: Testing the idea with real buyers.
paras: The positioning rests on one assumption: that people would pay more for a shawl they can trust. Next is a short survey of 10–20 people on how they choose a shawl and what would convince them it’s handwoven, and a source for weaving time so the record can carry it.
